newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - UK rates seen steady up to election.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - UK rates seen steady up to election.

text.p: British interest rates are likely to remain unchanged at six percent for now, but could rise shortly after the imminent election, a Reuters survey showed on Friday.

Twenty London-based economists were unanimous in their prediction of no change in interest rates at next Wednesday's monthly monetary meeting between Bank of England Governor Eddie George and Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke.
The economists said Clarke, who has the final say on setting rates, would be unwilling to increase the cost of borrowing so close to a parliamentary election, which must be held by May 22.
High levels of property ownership in Britain make the official rate offered by the Bank of England for borrowing or lending money of intense public interest and a potent political tool.
The economists said the chancellor would be particularly reluctant to raise rates given the dismal showing for his ruling Conservative party in a by-election on Thursday.
The opposition Labour party won the Wirral South by-election with a majority of 7,888 votes, reversing a Conservative majority of 8,183 at the last election in 1992.
Recent opinion polls, including a Reuters/NOP survey released on Tuesday, show Labour with around a 20 percentage point lead nationally over the Conservative party.

"The political restraints are intensified by last night's results. On a fundamental basis, the ongoing strength of sterling is also significant to the argument," said James Stewart, economist at S-E Banken in London.
Recent sterling strength has eased pressure on Clarke to raise rates -- sterling hit a 52-month high against the mark earlier this month and is still firm.

George's advice at recent meetings with Clarke has been for a small upward rise to keep inflationary pressure at bay. All of the economists surveyed said they expected George's position to prevail after the election.
Nineteen predicted an incoming chancellor would raise rates by the end of June. One forecast the new government would wait until July.

The economists were nearly equally split in their prediction over the size of the hike once it comes -- 11 said the increase would be of 25 basis points, and nine forecast a rise in the base rate to 6.50 percent.

"If it's a Labour administration, which seems pretty likely given yesterday's by-election result, it would try to convince the market of its determination to rein in inflation," said Ken Wattret, economist with Paribas.
"A 50-basis point rise would be a possibility, although our central case is for a 25-point rise," he said.

"Labour would raise rates after the election...but it would take a month to sort themselves out. We might have to wait until a mini-budget is passed. It would all depend on the sterling mood as well," said Mark Ramsden, UK economist at Stone and McCarthy.
